_comment: Synthetic corpus of coding-agent-style memories, hand-authored for the rAIminiscence vs hippo-memory Recall@k/Precision@k benchmark. `id` is the shared ground-truth key used by queries.json; `kind` follows rAIminiscence's MemoryKind (episodic/semantic/decision) and is mapped into hippo-memory's schema by the hippo runner (see benchmarks/README.md for the mapping table). Several pairs are deliberate near-duplicates or confusable siblings (same topic, different specifics) so naive exact-keyword matching alone is not sufficient to score well.

memories.content: The auth middleware validates JWTs in src/auth/middleware.ts.
JWT validation happens in the auth middleware at src/auth/middleware.ts, checking the exp and iss claims on every request.
Session cookies are set by a separate auth middleware in src/auth/session.ts, unrelated to JWT handling.
Prefer named exports over default exports in this repo.
This repo's lint config forbids default exports; named exports are required for all new modules.
React page components under src/pages/ are the one exception allowed to use default exports, for framework compatibility.
The CI pipeline times out after 10 minutes on the integration suite.
Integration tests run in CI with a 10 minute timeout; flaky tests are automatically retried twice before failing the build.
The unit test suite in CI completes in under 2 minutes, well within its separate budget.
We chose Postgres for the write model.
Postgres was selected over MySQL for the write model, mainly for its native JSONB support.
Redis is used for the read-through cache layer in front of Postgres.
The build uses webpack for bundling.
webpack.config.js defines separate entry points for the admin bundle and the public bundle.
ESLint config extends airbnb-base with custom overrides in .eslintrc.js.
Prettier is configured with a 100-character line width and double quotes.
API rate limiting is enforced at 100 requests per minute per API key in src/middleware/rateLimit.ts.
src/middleware/rateLimit.ts throttles requests using a token bucket algorithm, refilled once per second.
Deploys go through GitHub Actions to a staging environment before production.
Production deploys require a manual approval step in GitHub Actions after staging succeeds.
The onboarding docs for new engineers live in docs/onboarding.md.
Feature flags are managed via LaunchDarkly; the client wrapper is in src/flags/launchdarkly.ts.
Error logs are shipped to Sentry with release tagging enabled.
The team decided to migrate the test runner from Jest to Vitest for faster local test runs.
Vitest replaced Jest as the project's test runner; its config lives in vitest.config.ts.
Database migrations are managed with Prisma; run `npx prisma migrate dev` to apply pending ones.
The staging environment mirrors production infrastructure but is seeded with synthetic data.
Structured logs are emitted as JSON via pino, with a requestId field added by middleware.
The logging middleware (pino-based) attaches a requestId and userId to every JSON log line for correlation.
Log levels are configurable per-environment via LOG_LEVEL; production defaults to 'info'.
Alerts for elevated error rates are configured in Datadog, paging the on-call engineer via PagerDuty.
The on-call rotation for production incidents is managed in PagerDuty with weekly handoffs.
Datadog dashboards track p95 latency per endpoint, refreshed every minute.
Outbound HTTP calls retry up to 3 times with exponential backoff starting at 200ms.
The retry/backoff logic for outbound calls lives in src/lib/httpClient.ts and is shared by every service client.
Webhook deliveries are retried by the third-party provider, not by our own code.
Background jobs run through a BullMQ queue backed by Redis.
BullMQ workers process the email-sending queue with a concurrency of 5.
Redis also backs session storage for logged-in users, unrelated to the job queue.
Secrets are stored in AWS Secrets Manager and injected as environment variables at deploy time, replacing the old .env-in-repo approach.
AWS Secrets Manager rotates the database credentials automatically every 30 days.
A .env.example file documents which environment variables are required locally, but real secrets never live in the repo.
The production Docker image is built from a multi-stage Dockerfile using node:22-alpine as the final base.
The Dockerfile's builder stage installs devDependencies and compiles TypeScript; the final stage copies only the compiled output.
Local development uses docker-compose to run Postgres and Redis alongside the app.
API versioning is done via a URL prefix (/v1/, /v2/) rather than a header, for easier debugging and caching.
/v1/ endpoints are frozen and only receive security patches; new features land under /v2/.
An internal-only /admin/ prefix exists for tooling endpoints, unrelated to the public API's version scheme.
Pull requests require at least one approval and a passing CI run before merge; two approvals are required for changes under src/auth/.
The code review checklist in CONTRIBUTING.md asks reviewers to check for test coverage and updated docs.
A bot automatically assigns a random reviewer from the on-call rotation if no one claims a PR within a day.
New features roll out behind a feature flag at 5% traffic first, ramping to 100% over a week if error rates stay flat.
Feature flag percentages are configured per-flag in LaunchDarkly's targeting rules, not in application code.
A flag left permanently at 50% for over six months was cleaned up and hard-coded to 'on' during a tech-debt sprint.
Dependency upgrades are batched monthly via a single PR from Renovate, except for security patches which land immediately.
Renovate is configured to group all non-major devDependency bumps into one monthly PR.
A major version bump of React was done manually, outside Renovate's normal batching, because it needed a migration guide.
